gaps.sentence: He passed all his exams first time, ___ surprised everyone.
gaps.hint: refers to the whole previous clause
gaps.explanation: 'Which' can refer to a whole idea ('he passed first time'); this non-defining use never takes 'that'.

gaps.sentence: The exam, the results of ___ will be published on Friday, was very difficult.
gaps.hint: quantity noun + of + thing in a non-defining clause
gaps.explanation: 'The results of which' joins the clauses formally; 'of whom' is for people and 'of them' cannot link clauses after a comma.

gaps.sentence: The chair on ___ the cat was sleeping was my grandmother's.
gaps.explanation: 'On which' is the formal pattern for things; 'on where' and 'on that' are not grammatical.

gaps.sentence: I'll never forget the day ___ we first met.
gaps.explanation: 'When' replaces 'on which' after time nouns like day, year and moment.

gaps.sentence: That's the office ___ I worked for ten years.
gaps.explanation: 'Where' means 'in which'; 'I worked the office' shows the place role of the gap.

gaps.sentence: The house at the end of the street, ___ has been empty for years, is for sale.
gaps.explanation: Non-defining clauses about things take 'which'; 'who' is for people and 'that' is not allowed here.

gaps.sentence: Pablo, ___ speaks five languages, works as an interpreter.
gaps.explanation: Non-defining clauses about people take 'who'; 'that' never follows a comma in standard English.

gaps.sentence: The man ___ lives next door is a doctor.
gaps.explanation: 'Who' refers to people as the subject of the clause; 'which' is for things and 'whose' shows possession.
